studentFacing: Your essay has a clear overall idea: asking other people gives you more ideas and better choices. You also use some linking words such as 'Therefore', 'However' and 'Like if...' to move between points. However, the ideas do not always connect smoothly. The middle paragraph about behaving in class jumps to a new story, and the ending of that paragraph about a leader does not clearly link back to your main point. The headings ('Manner-better choices', 'Tone- expiring') do not seem to match what follows. Try starting each paragraph with a topic sentence that links to your thesis, and finish with a sentence that explains how your example proves your point.

You try a range of sentence types, including sentences with 'because', 'if' and 'Then' clauses. Several sentences become confusing or incomplete because the structure breaks down, for example the sentence fragment 'The other students that are working with you on the class project they can come up with new details'. This sentence has two subjects and no clear connection. Some sentences are also very long and repeat the same structure. Try reading each sentence aloud and splitting long ones. Check that each clause has a clear subject and verb and that clauses are joined properly.

Your word choice is simple and mostly understandable, and you do use some topic words like 'advice', 'behave' and 'leader'. However, you repeat the same words often ('ideas', 'main ideas', 'project', 'good'), and some words are not precise. For example, 'a good way' and 'a lot smarter' are quite general. Try replacing repeated words with more exact ones, such as 'suggestions', 'perspectives', 'collaborate' or 'contribute', and explain your points with more specific words.

You use some natural phrases such as 'come up with', 'make a better choice' and 'figure out'. These help your writing sound natural. A few expressions are not quite idiomatic, such as 'gave you an advice' ('advice' is uncountable, so say 'gave you advice') and 'every one will many ideas', where words are missing. Also, 'Seeking multiple options' does not fit well with the topic of asking for opinions; 'seeking multiple opinions' would be more accurate. Keep practising common word combinations and check them in a dictionary or example sentences.

Your meaning is usually clear, but there are frequent grammar errors that make reading harder. These include your/you're confusion ('your being bad', 'Your going to have to'), verb tense and form problems ('Therefore you were writing', 'if your were doing'), missing words ('every one will many ideas'), article errors ('a idea'), and 'you project' instead of 'your project'. Proofread slowly for these patterns. Check each 'your' by asking whether it can be replaced by 'you are'. Keep to one tense, probably present, when giving general advice.

There are several convention errors. Apostrophes are missing or misused ('cant', 'its', 'thats', 'your' for 'you're'). 'Therefor' is misspelled and should be 'Therefore', and 'hunted house' should be 'haunted house'. Spacing after commas is sometimes missing ('ideas,something'). Also, 'Therefore' and 'However' should usually be followed by a comma. Make a checklist for apostrophes, commas after linking words and commonly confused words, and check these when you edit.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear plan: each paragraph covers one sport (soccer, track, basketball, softball), and you use 'The first one,' 'The second one,' and 'The next one' to move between them. That helps the reader follow you. Within paragraphs, though, ideas sometimes jump around. In the soccer paragraph you move from tricks to soccer's popularity to the name 'football' without linking them. The ending ('Thats why of all the sport my favorite is track') also doesn't connect well to your opening idea about talents. Try a thesis sentence at the start and a conclusion that returns to it. Add transitions that explain how one idea leads to the next.

You try a mix of simple, compound and complex sentences, such as the 'because' sentences, which is good. Some sentences run together without proper joining, so the reader can't tell where one idea stops and the next begins. Try splitting these or joining them with a conjunction or a semicolon. Reading your work aloud will help you hear where to pause.

Your word choice is mostly everyday and clear, and a few phrases show personality, like 'your mind goes blank' and 'it's like flying.' Several words are very general, such as 'everything,' 'thing,' 'big,' and 'good.' Try more precise words, for example 'popular' instead of 'big' and 'beneficial' or 'strengthens' instead of 'good arm excise.' Using specific details about how each sport feels or looks would also strengthen your writing.

You use some natural expressions, like 'in my opinion' and 'out of the house.' A few phrases don't sound quite right in English, and fixing them will make your writing more fluent. For example, 'in the England' should be 'in England,' and 'Soccer isn't big as well know as it should be' should be 'Soccer isn't as well known as it should be.' 'Seen's I was little' should be 'since I was little.'

Your meaning usually comes through, but there are repeated errors in verb tense and form, articles, and missing words. Check these: 'I been doing it' should be 'I have been doing it'; 'the boys ad girls' should be 'the boys and girls'; 'The thing about is' is missing a word; 'I think is unfair' should be 'I think it is unfair'; and 'help me' should be 'helps me.' Also check that 'it' refers to something clear when you say 'doing it' for several sports ('them').

There are a number of spelling, punctuation and capitalisation slips that proofreading would catch. Examples: extra or misplaced commas and spaces ('basketball ,softball,, track'), a missing apostrophe ('thats'), a lowercase sentence start ('basketball because...'), and misspellings ('seen's' for 'since,' 'excise' for 'exercise,' 'he boys' for 'the boys,' 'assonstion' for 'association'). Read your essay once just for punctuation and once just for spelling before you finish.

studentFacing: Your central idea is clear and you come back to it at the end: attitude is the key to success. However, the essay is one long block with no paragraphs, and few linking words guide the reader from one idea to the next. Your teacher example is a good way to support your point, but it needs an introduction and a clear conclusion. Try splitting the essay into an introduction, two or three body paragraphs (work, home, friends), and a conclusion. Use transitions such as 'for example', 'however', 'as a result'.

Most of your sentences run together without a break, so it is hard to see where one idea ends and another starts. You often repeat the pattern 'if you control your attitude, you control...'. This repetition is effective once or twice, but try varying your sentences: some short, some longer with 'because', 'although', or 'when'. Separating each idea into its own sentence will help you control your structures.

You use simple, understandable words, and 'attitude', 'success', and 'control' are the right key words. You repeat them very often, though. Try adding more precise words, such as 'behavior', 'reputation', 'patience', 'achieve', 'positive/negative', or 'temper', instead of 'good' and 'bad' each time.

Some phrases are natural, such as 'the key to success' and 'lose your friends'. Others need a different preposition or word choice. We say 'the key to your success', not 'key of'. We say 'get angry easily', 'say something mean to', and 'make a lot of friends'. Learning these word partnerships will make your writing sound more natural.

Your meaning is usually understandable, but there are frequent errors in word forms, verbs, and agreement. Examples: 'you will never success' needs the noun/verb form 'succeed'; 'you most know' should be 'you must know'; 'your get hiring' should be 'you get hired'; 'your' is used where 'you' or 'you're' is needed; and 'it not good' needs 'is not good'. Reread each sentence and check the subject, the verb, and the word form.

The essay has almost no punctuation or capitalization, which makes it hard to read. Start each sentence with a capital letter and end it with a period. The word 'I' and the first word of each sentence should be capitalized. There are also several spelling errors. Reading your work aloud and then checking spelling can help you find them, for example 'nicily' (nicely), 'angery' (angry), 'parant' (parent), 'easlier' (easier), 'contron' (control), 'while' (whole).

Paragraph 3 is one very long chain of 'and' clauses, so the ideas blur together. The last body paragraph moves from challenges to being liked by more people without explaining the connection. Try using transitions such as 'for example', 'as a result' or 'in contrast' to show how each idea leads to the next. Add a specific example, such as a person who failed repeatedly before succeeding, to anchor each paragraph.

You use some complex sentences with 'because' and 'when', which is a good start. Many sentences are very long and joined only by 'and', and a few run together without proper boundaries. Your sentence variety would improve if you split long sentences and mixed in short, direct ones. Try also using relative clauses or an opening phrase, for example 'Although failure is uncomfortable, it teaches us...'.

Your word choice is clear and easy to follow, but it is quite general and repetitive. 'Fail', 'success', 'life' and 'things' appear many times. Try more precise words such as 'setback', 'perseverance', 'resilience', 'determination' or 'accomplish'. Replacing vague phrases like 'a big thing' and 'try things' with exact words will make your ideas stronger.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'take those challenges head on', 'second chance' and 'giving up is not an option'. Some phrases are slightly off, and a few collocations need fixing. We say 'in the pursuit of success', not 'On the pursuit'. 'A great price' is probably meant to be 'a great prize' or 'reward'. 'Without loss of enthusiasm' and 'can help be successful' also need smoother phrasing, such as 'can help you become successful'.

Your meaning usually comes through, but several recurring errors affect clarity. Watch 'does' used instead of 'those', verb forms and missing words, and singular/plural agreement. Check each sentence for a subject, a correct verb and any missing words.

- 'does mistakes comes' → 'those mistakes comes' needs 'those mistakes come'
- 'you have to happy' → 'you have to be happy'
- 'the only get it' → 'they only get it'
- 'try new thing' → 'try new things'
- 'it takes the a few times' → 'it takes a few times'
- 'try again and be successful' → 'try again and become successful'

Your capitalisation is mostly correct and you use paragraphs. Spelling and punctuation need attention. 'form' is used where you mean 'from', and 'strait away' should be 'straight away'. 'an' should be 'and' in one place. There is also a misplaced comma, and some sentences need full stops or commas where clauses run together. Proofreading aloud will help you catch these.

That is a strong start. Often the links between sentences are missing or unclear, so the reader has to guess how one idea leads to the next. Transitions like 'In the other hand' and 'In a other hand' don't show a real contrast, because the ideas are adding to each other. Try 'Another example is...' or 'For instance'. The last paragraph is one long run of ideas, so split it into separate sentences and say what each one adds. A closing sentence that returns to your main point would also help.

You try some longer sentences with 'but', 'when' and 'that', which shows you want to vary your writing. Many of these sentences run together without a clear break or connecting word, so they become run-ons. Practise finding where one complete idea ends and the next begins, then use a period or a connector like 'because' or 'so'. Reading your work aloud will help you hear where to pause. Also try mixing in short, clear sentences with the longer ones.

Your word choices are simple and mostly clear, and words like 'successes', 'respect' and 'difficult time' fit your topic. Some words are confused with others that sound similar or are the wrong word for the meaning. Check these carefully, since they change the meaning of your sentence. Try adding more specific words, such as 'encouraging', 'kind' or 'positive', in place of repeating 'good' and 'bad'.

You use some common phrases, like 'make people feel good', 'make new friends' and 'show a smile'. Several expressions are not quite standard, so they sound unusual to a reader. For example, 'at less' should be 'at least', and 'In the other hand' is normally 'On the other hand'. Learn these set phrases as whole units. 'Had a bad day' is also a good phrase, and you can use it consistently.

Look at 'good attitude make' (it should be 'makes'), 'we seen' (should be 'we saw'), and 'she cant so we want to help' (the tense and logic need fixing: 'she couldn't, so we wanted to help' or 'she was struggling, so we helped'). Also check small words like articles ('a other' should be 'another') and pronouns ('is hand' should be 'his hand'; 'your mad' should be 'you're mad'). Re-read each sentence and ask: Who is doing the action, and when did it happen?

You use paragraphs and end your ideas with some punctuation, which is good. Spelling, capitalization and punctuation need more attention. Always capitalize the word 'I' and the first word of each sentence. Put a space after commas and use a period at the end of each complete thought. Many spelling mistakes come from words that sound like the right word, so proofread slowly and use a dictionary or spell check. Look at 'cant' (can't), 'bother' (brother), 'bed' (bad), 'rode' (road), 'waling' (walking), 'bast' (best), and 'batter' (better).

studentFacing: You organised your essay into clear paragraphs and used helpful transition words such as 'To begin with', 'In addition', 'Also' and 'In conclusion'. However, the paragraphs repeat the same idea (Einstein was smart, so he must have had imagination) instead of building an argument. The sentences within paragraphs are often linked only by repeating words like 'really smart' and 'a lot'. Try giving each body paragraph one new reason and linking your sentences with words that show cause and effect, such as 'therefore' or 'as a result'.

You use some complex sentences with 'because' and 'so', which is a good start. Several sentences are run-ons, where two or more complete ideas are joined with only a comma or with no punctuation. Practise splitting long sentences or joining them correctly with a conjunction or a semicolon. Also try varying how your sentences begin, since many start with 'Elbert Einstein'.

Your word choice is simple and mostly understandable, but it repeats a lot. 'Really smart', 'a lot' and 'cool' appear many times. More precise words would make your ideas stronger, for example 'brilliant', 'innovative', 'creative' or 'groundbreaking' instead of 'really smart' and 'cool'. Try to name Einstein's actual achievements, such as the theory of relativity, instead of calling them 'inventions and gadgets'. You also confuse 'genus' with 'genius'.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'lived through a lot' and 'Use your imagination'. Some word combinations sound unusual or are incomplete. For example, 'a wild imagination' works, but 'at you school' and 'o with your family' do not. Try learning common collocations like 'a vivid imagination', 'come up with ideas', 'make a discovery' and 'play an important role'. These will make your writing sound more natural.

Some of your grammar is controlled well, such as 'he was one of the smartest human beings'. There are several errors to work on. In your first paragraph, 'now imagination than' should be 'no imagination, then'. 'A lot of thing' needs the plural 'things'. 'To make to things' should be 'to make things'. 'Genus' should be 'genius'. 'You can use your imagination to become a genus at you school' needs 'your' and 'genius'. Reading your essay aloud slowly can help you catch these mistakes.

You start your sentences with capital letters and end most of them with full stops, which is good. However, Einstein's first name is spelled inconsistently ('Albert' and 'Elbert'). Always check the spelling of names, especially when the name appears in your prompt. You also need commas before and after clauses (for example, after 'Also' phrases and before 'that is why'). Watch for extra spaces inside quotation marks, and for typos like 'o' instead of 'or'. Finally, the question mark in your opening should be followed by a clear answer sentence.

studentFacing: You have a clear plan: an introduction, one paragraph about the park and one about the beach. Phrases like 'One of the activities' and 'Another way' help the reader follow it. Inside the paragraphs, though, the ideas drift and the links are weak. 'And also' is repeated many times, and the sentence about the 'second point' is confusing because you never state what the first and second points are. The introduction also lacks a clear position, and there is no conclusion. Try a topic sentence for each paragraph, then link your examples with varied transitions such as 'for instance', 'in addition' and 'as a result'. Finish with a short closing paragraph.

You try some longer sentences with several clauses, which is a good sign. Many of them run on without clear boundaries, so the reader can't tell where one idea ends and the next begins. The long park sentence joins at least four ideas without punctuation. Some sentences also start with 'and also' as if they continued the previous one. Split long sentences into two or three shorter ones, then practise combining them with 'who', 'which', 'because' or 'while'.

Your word choice is understandable and fits the topic (park, beach, dog, free time). It is also repetitive and general. 'Fun' appears many times, and 'things' and 'stuff' are vague. Try more precise words, for example 'relaxing', 'refreshing', 'socialise', 'unwind', 'recreation' and 'stressful'. Replace 'stuff on your shoulder' with a specific noun such as 'work pressure'.

Some phrases are natural, such as 'clear your mind', 'free time' and 'make friends'. Others are not quite idiomatic or are awkward. For example, 'leave their life the way they want to' is unclear, and 'on your shoulder' should be 'on your shoulders' or, better, 'weighing on your mind'. 'Alone time on their own' is redundant. 'The best time of his or her life' is a strong fixed phrase but is used somewhat loosely. Notice the collocations you read and use them: 'spend time outdoors', 'enjoy the fresh air', 'take a break from work'.

Your meaning usually comes through, but several grammar problems get in the way. 'They are many things' should be 'There are many things'. There are pronoun and agreement slips: 'one, or a family can spend their time', and 'have fun with them' where 'them' is unclear. Some words are wrong or missing: 'with the' should be 'with them', 'al' should be 'all', and 'the area of the park they are' needs 'where they are'. 'Someone will have interest' would be more natural as 'someone might be interested in'. Reread each sentence and check the subject, the verb, and what each pronoun refers to.

Spelling is mostly correct, but punctuation and capitalisation need attention. Spaces are missing after commas ('jump,catch things,and'), and many long sentences have no commas or full stops where they're needed. A sentence begins with a lowercase letter after a full stop ('and also if they go alone'), and 'i' is not capitalised. There are typos ('al', 'with the'). Proofread aloud, put a full stop wherever you pause for a new idea, and leave a space after every comma.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear structure: you state the quote, give your opinion, and then give two examples, and you end with a concluding sentence. Transitions such as 'For example', 'Another example', 'So' and 'After that' help the reader follow the order of events. However, the link between the quote and your reasoning is weak. The sentence 'Because he didn't give up to write a statement' does not clearly connect to Emerson's idea about trying things beyond what you have mastered. Repeating 'give up' and 'Generic_Name' or 'she' many times also makes the paragraphs feel repetitive. Try linking each example back to the quote (for example, explain what the new challenge was and how it caused growth), and use a wider range of connectors such as 'however', 'as a result' and 'in contrast'. Your conclusion is very short, so try to restate your main idea and explain why it matters.

Most of your sentences are short and simple, and many start with 'So', 'But', 'Also' or 'After'. You do show some variety, for example with the 'If...' conditional sentences and the sentence 'She studied hard, and researched how to succeed in the experiment.' Try combining short sentences with subordinate clauses ('Although she wanted to quit, she kept studying...'), and avoid sentence fragments such as 'Because he didn't give up to write a statement.' and 'Another example, Generic_Name wants to be a scientist.' Practise relative clauses and participial phrases to add range.

Your vocabulary is simple but generally understandable, and you use topic words such as 'scientist', 'laboratory', 'experiment' and 'driver's license'. Some words are repeated often ('give up', 'hard', 'job') and some are imprecise, such as 'experiment materials', 'hard science problems' and 'easy way'. Try more precise alternatives: 'persevere', 'challenging', 'equipment', 'career', 'take the easy option', 'overcome obstacles', 'determination'. Using words like 'comfort zone' or 'growth' would also connect your examples to the quotation.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'give up', 'took the driving lesson', 'got a driver's license' and 'succeed in'. There are several collocation and preposition problems, though. In English we say 'wanted to give up the driving lessons' or 'wanted to give up on...', 'take driving lessons', 'work hard at her job', 'get a job as a scientist', 'in an easier way', and 'decided not to give up'. Learning these word partnerships as chunks will make your writing sound more natural. 'Gonna' is also too informal for an essay.

Your basic sentence patterns are clear, and you use past tense correctly in many places ('he didn't give up', 'took', 'got'). Common errors to work on: (1) tense consistency, because you shift between past and present in the same story ('After he got a driver's license, he can drive' should be 'he could drive'; 'wants' and 'wanted'); (2) verb patterns ('decided to don't give up' should be 'decided not to give up'; 'didn't give up to write' needs a different structure); (3) articles and countability ('studying a science' should be 'studying science'; 'a job scientist' should be 'a job as a scientist'); (4) word form and adverbs ('doing hard' should be 'working hard'; 'a job that can do easy way' should be 'a job that is easier'). Also 'I agree with his statement' is correct, but the following reason sentence needs a complete clause.

Your spelling is accurate and you capitalise sentences and use quotation marks correctly for the quotes. The main issue is comma use: you often put a comma after sentence-starting words ('But,', 'So,') or before 'and' with no need ('She studied hard, and researched...'; 'many hard science problems, and experiment materials'). Remove commas that separate a verb from its object or join two items. Also avoid starting sentences with 'Because' on their own, which creates fragments. Check that you use 'a driver's license' and apostrophes consistently, which you do well.

studentFacing: Your ideas are in short separate lines, and it is hard to see how they connect. You start with introductions, then talk about community, then about English. Try adding linking words such as 'because', 'for example', 'also' and 'finally'. Group related sentences in paragraphs. Your example 'ex: my idea is to respect the teacher and other people' is a good start, because it tries to support your idea. Write it as a full sentence: 'For example, my idea is to respect the teacher and other people.'

You mostly use very short, simple sentences. Some sentences are incomplete. For example, 'Because...' begins a sentence but does not connect to a main idea. Try joining it to the sentence before: 'The community is very important because it teaches people good ideas.' Also, 'am coming from' is missing the subject 'I'. Practise combining two simple ideas into one longer sentence.

You use basic words that communicate your main ideas, such as 'community', 'respect', 'student' and 'important'. 'Respect' is a good word choice. To improve, add more specific words to explain why the community is important (for example 'support', 'values', 'learn from'). Also check word choice: 'teacher' is used as a verb, but the verb is 'teach'.

Some expressions are not natural in English. We say 'I am a student at SCHOOL_NAME in 8th grade' and 'I don't speak English well'. We say 'in my country' and not 'to my contry'. Learning common phrases like 'good at', 'in my country', 'a good idea' will help. You can note useful phrases when you read.

There are several grammar patterns to work on. Verb forms: 'am coming' should be 'I come' or 'I am from'. Negatives: 'I don't no speak' should be 'I don't speak'. Adverb: 'English good' should be 'English well'. Pronouns: 'he' for 'community' should be 'it'. Verb: 'teacher' should be 'teaches'. Missing verb: 'Because to my contry no English' needs 'there is no English' or 'English is not spoken'. Check each sentence for a subject and a verb.

You use some capital letters and full stops correctly. Remember to capitalise 'I' every time and the first word of each sentence, such as 'my' and 'i'. 'Contry' should be spelled 'country', 'don't no' should be 'don't know' if you meant that word, and '8grade' should be '8th grade'. 'Thank's' should be 'Thanks' with no apostrophe. Put a full stop or comma after 'Dear friend' (a comma is usual) and 'other' needs a noun after it, such as 'other subjects'.

Some links between ideas are abrupt, though. The question at the end of the first paragraph is hard to follow, and the final paragraph repeats the same sentence pattern rather than building on your earlier points. Try linking each paragraph to the one before it with a transition, and use your conclusion to pull your ideas together rather than restating them.

You use a mix of simple and longer sentences and begin to use subordinate clauses with 'because'. Many longer sentences run together without proper punctuation or conjunctions (run-ons), which makes them hard to read. Try splitting these into two or three sentences, or joining them with a conjunction or a semicolon. Varying how you start sentences would also help, since several in a row begin with 'Wis people'.

Your vocabulary is mostly simple, but it is clear, and you use some stronger words such as 'impacted', 'regret', and 'successful'. The word 'wis' is repeated very often. Try 'wise', 'insight', 'advice', or 'guidance' to make your meaning more precise and avoid repetition. Words like 'thing' and 'a lot' could also be replaced with more specific choices.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'fight through', 'never give up', and 'change someone's day'. A few phrases sound unnatural or don't fit together well, so check how words are usually combined. For example, 'the key of life' is usually 'the key to life', and 'shut anything in your brain' could be 'shut out your thoughts'. Reading your work aloud can help you spot phrases that sound off.

Your meaning usually comes through, but there are recurring grammar errors. Watch your verb forms and tense ('has anyone gave you' should be 'has anyone given you'; 'change' should be 'changed'). Check word forms too, such as 'your' versus 'you're' and 'wis' versus 'wise'. 'Any wonder why' should be 'I wonder why'. Proofreading for verb tense and word choice after drafting would help a lot.

Several spelling errors repeat, and punctuation needs attention. Words like 'suddenly', 'relieved', 'actually', 'remember', and 'opposite' are misspelled, and 'wise' is spelled 'wis' throughout. Start each sentence with a capital letter (after 'Has anyone ever shared wisdom with you?' you wrote 'well' in lowercase). Use commas and full stops to separate ideas, and put commas before or after quotations. Keeping a list of words you often misspell and checking them before you finish will help.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear plan in the first paragraph: three reasons (lost focus, tired teachers, students changing schools). The body does not follow that plan clearly, though. The second paragraph stops in the middle ('for instance') and the long third paragraph mixes all your reasons together. Try one paragraph per reason, each starting with a topic sentence and using transitions such as 'First,' 'Another reason,' and 'Finally.' Your conclusion also needs to restate your position instead of asking the reader to imagine something.

You try many kinds of sentences, including ones with 'because', 'once', and 'if'. Many sentences run together without punctuation or connecting words, so it is hard to see where one idea ends and the next begins. Try splitting long sentences in two, or join ideas with a clear connector. For example: 'Once students get tired, they lose focus. They start talking with each other.'

You use relevant words like 'focus', 'extend', 'drop out', and 'decision maker', and your examples are specific. Some words are repeated a lot ('tired', 'get tired') and a few are confused with words that sound similar. Check words like 'taxing' (texting), 'panning' (planning), 'sanding' (standing), 'think' (thing), and 'bad rooms' (bathrooms?). Using synonyms such as 'exhausted', 'distracted', or 'overwhelmed' would add variety.

Some of your phrases are natural, such as 'get tired of', 'drop out of', and 'a day'. Others need different word combinations. English says 'lose focus', 'take care of', 'at the usual time', and 'for many reasons'. Learning common phrases like these as whole units will help.

The most frequent issue is verb form after 'will' and after subjects. After 'will' use the base verb: 'will lose', 'will talk', 'will use', 'will listen'. Also check subject-verb agreement ('schools was', 'they doesnt', 'those who works') and plurals ('many reason', 'some of the student', 'two hundred student'). Also watch 'form' vs 'from' and 'than' vs 'then'. Reread each verb after 'will' as a final check.

Capitalization and punctuation need attention. Always capitalize 'I' and proper names ('United States', 'Afghanistan' is already correct). Start each sentence with a capital letter. Add commas after introductory words ('In addition,' 'However,') and apostrophes in contractions ('can't', 'doesn't'). Spelling errors like 'where' for 'were', 'form' for 'from', 'ever' for 'every', and 'o clock' also need checking. Reading your essay aloud slowly can help you find where periods belong.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear overall structure: an introduction, body paragraphs, a counter-argument paragraph and a conclusion. The Batman and Joker example is a good way to support your claim. However, ideas repeat often, especially in the last two paragraphs, where the same sentence about good traits leading to success appears almost word for word twice. Some links between sentences are also unclear, for example the idea that the journey matters more than the destination does not connect clearly to your argument. Try to give each paragraph one main idea, add new evidence instead of repeating, and use linking words (for instance 'however', 'as a result', 'for example') to show how one point leads to the next.

You try a range of structures, including 'Although...' openings, 'while' clauses and conditionals. This is a good sign. But many sentences run on without punctuation or are incomplete, which makes the meaning hard to follow. Some sentences that begin with 'Although' or 'Even though' never finish with a main clause, and others join too many ideas together. Practise splitting long sentences into two and always check that a subordinate clause is attached to a main clause.

Your vocabulary is understandable and fits the topic (traits, honest, trustworthy, consequences). However, it is quite limited and repetitive. 'Worst', 'bad', 'good' and 'traits' appear very many times, and 'worst' is often used where 'bad' or 'negative' is needed. Try to use more precise words such as 'destructive', 'admirable', 'integrity', 'resilience' or 'deceitful', and vary your wording so you do not repeat the same phrase.

There are some natural expressions, such as 'Trust is like a glass if it breaks it will never be the same' and 'We write our stories by ourselves'. These make your writing more vivid. However, several collocations and fixed phrases are not quite right. For example, 'a process of learning', 'adapt good traits' (the usual word is 'adopt') and 'reflect on our future selves' do not sound natural. 'Most of times' should be 'most of the time'. Also, 'by ourselves' is often used where 'for ourselves' or simply 'we choose' would sound more natural. Reading model essays and noting common phrases will help.

Grammar is the area that needs the most attention. Subject-verb agreement is often incorrect ('traits ... comes', 'bad experiences doesn't give'). There are also word form and missing-word errors ('formed' without 'be', 'than' instead of 'then', 'depends on our', 'ours characters', 'rather that'). Articles and pronouns are sometimes wrong too ('a worst trait', 'it past is past', 'change their selves'). After you finish writing, reread slowly and check each verb against its subject, and check that every sentence has all the words it needs.

Spelling is mostly correct, and you start sentences with capital letters. The main problems are punctuation. Commas are often missing after introductory phrases and before 'for example', and there are missing spaces after commas. The apostrophe is missing in 'its' (it's), and quotation marks are used in a way that is not clear. Some sentence fragments are punctuated as full sentences. Also check that you add a comma after 'In conclusion' and use full stops to separate long strings of ideas.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear structure: an introduction, three body paragraphs that each start with a signpost ("First of all", "Second reason", "Another reason"), and a conclusion. That makes your argument easy to follow. Inside the paragraphs, the links between sentences are weaker. "By the way" is a casual phrase for changing the subject, so it does not fit as a transition into your main point. The conclusion also adds a new idea (the SAT) after you have already summed up, which breaks the flow. Try to put every reason in the body, and use transitions like "for instance", "as a result" or "in addition" to join your sentences.

You use a mix of simple, compound and complex sentences, including conditionals ("If this student already decided...") and relative clauses. This shows you are trying a range of structures. Several longer sentences lose control, though, because the structure is incomplete or tangled. Reading these sentences aloud and splitting very long ones into two will help.

Your vocabulary is understandable and fits the topic ("career", "freshman or sophomore year", "opportunites"). It is quite repetitive, though. You use "good", "college/university" and "career" many times. Some word choices are not precise, such as "get fun", and there is some word-form confusion ("effects" for "affects"). Try synonyms and more exact words, for example "enjoy themselves", "higher education", "profession" and "influences".

Some phrases are natural and correct, such as "save money" and "in conclusion". Others use the wrong preposition or an unusual word combination. Learning common collocations as whole chunks will help, for example "attend college", "depend on", "make a decision", "in this kind of situation" and "pay for".

Your ideas come across, but some grammar errors are repeated. The main patterns are: (1) verb forms after "to" or a preposition, where you need an -ing form or the infinitive ("graduate in three years... would be good" should be "graduating... would be good"); (2) subject-verb agreement ("students who doesn't have money", "their careers is"); (3) articles ("a extra year" should be "an extra year"); (4) tense and form errors ("graduateded", "scientistists"); and (5) pronoun use ("this student... he" should be consistent, or use "they"). Proofread once for each pattern in turn.

Your paragraphing and capitalisation are mostly good. There are several repeated spelling errors, especially "desicion" (it should be "decision"), plus "opportunites", "graduateded" and "scientistists". Punctuation is also uneven. You need commas after introductory phrases ("First of all," "In conclusion,") and the apostrophe in "childrens'" should be "children's". Also, a sentence should not start in the middle of a thought after a line break, as in the last paragraph. Keep a personal list of words you misspell and check it before you submit.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear position (students should wait until high school) and each paragraph returns to it. However, the ideas are joined mostly with 'also' and 'because', and some sentences run together so it is hard to see where one idea ends. Try using a wider range of transitions (for example 'however', 'for instance', 'as a result') and give each paragraph one main reason with an example. Also avoid repeating the same sentence idea in different paragraphs.

You try some longer sentences with 'because', 'so' and 'once', which is good. But many sentences join several ideas without a break (run-ons), and the structure sometimes breaks down midway. Practice splitting long sentences into two or three shorter ones, and then combine them with clear conjunctions or relative clauses. Vary how your sentences begin too.

Your word choice is clear and understandable, but it is repetitive. 'Career', 'young age' and 'find' appear many times. Try more precise words such as 'explore', 'decide on', 'interests', 'guidance counselor', 'distracted' or 'mature'. 'Brag' is a nice specific choice. Also take care with word forms like 'intresting' when you mean 'interested'.

Some phrases are natural, like 'at a young age' and 'in the future'. Others are not quite standard collocations, such as 'troubling time to find', 'talk to a counseling' and 'visit careers search'. Learn common phrases like 'have trouble finding', 'talk to a counselor', and 'use a career search tool'. Reading model essays can help you notice these word partnerships.

The most frequent issue is plural agreement: after 'a lot of', 'many', and 'student', use plural nouns ('students', 'careers') and matching verbs ('want', 'are'). There are also verb form errors ('haven't choose', 'haven't find'), confusion between 'there' and 'their', and 'they mind' instead of 'their minds'. Proofread specifically for plural -s endings and past participles. Your meaning is usually still clear.

Several conventions need attention. Capitalise 'I' every time and the first word of each sentence. Fix spelling: 'carrer', 'intrested/intresting', 'forcusing', 'thats'. Punctuation is a big issue: commas are used where full stops are needed, a double full stop appears at the end of paragraph two, and the apostrophe in 'that's' is missing. Read your essay aloud and put a full stop wherever you naturally pause at the end of an idea.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear structure: an introduction, body paragraphs that use signals like 'First reasons', 'Also' and 'However', and a conclusion. You also use 'For example' to bring in stories. However, the connection between your stories and your main idea is often unclear. For example, the story about your brother's wife failing the exam and the story about the shop robbery are not clearly linked back to the idea of continuing despite failure. Some sentences also run together, so the reader loses the thread. Try ending each paragraph with one sentence that says how the example proves your point. Also, check that pronouns like 'they', 'he' and 'her' clearly refer to the right person.

You try a range of sentence types, including sentences with 'because', 'so', 'if' and 'when'. The problem is control. Many sentences are very long and are joined with 'so' or 'and' without clear punctuation, which makes them hard to follow. Some sentences are also incomplete or have confused word order. Try splitting long sentences into two or three shorter ones, each with one main idea. Then practise joining them with a clear linking word.

Your vocabulary is mostly simple and repeated. Words like 'success', 'failure' and 'good' are used again and again, and sometimes in the wrong word form. There are also some word-choice mix-ups, such as 'discuss' where you probably mean 'decision' or 'discussion', and 'contusion' for 'conclusion'. Try to learn a few more precise words for this topic, such as 'persevere', 'determination', 'setback', 'motivation' and 'achieve'. Using them would make your ideas clearer.

You use some common expressions well, such as 'give up', 'no matter what' and 'made up your mind' (although it is spelled 'Maine'). Many other phrases are not quite natural English, so the meaning is unclear. Collocations (words that usually go together) are a good thing to practise. For example, say 'fail an exam', 'pass an exam', 'believe in yourself', 'lose enthusiasm' and 'in front of the shop'. Keeping a list of these phrases from your reading would help.

Grammar errors are frequent and sometimes make the meaning hard to understand. The main patterns are: (1) subject-verb agreement ('failure don't', 'it mean', 'people was'); (2) verb tense ('she get up', 'she fail her exam', 'I tell her'); (3) using the wrong word form, such as a noun for an adjective or verb ('you will be success', 'you will failure', 'you can loss'); and (4) pronoun forms ('they life', 'me exam', 'tell them self'). A useful habit is to reread and check each verb: is the subject singular or plural, and is the time past or present? Also say 'you will be successful' and 'you will fail'.

Some of your punctuation is right, and you use periods and commas in places. However, there are repeated convention problems. The capital 'I' is often written as lowercase 'l' (for example 'l agree'). There are also spelling errors such as 'preform', 'fist', 'believer', 'infant' (for 'in front'), and 'ever where'. Capital letters sometimes appear in the middle of sentences ('Some people', 'Most of the people'), and there are missing apostrophes ('am going', 'ls important'). Proofread slowly, line by line, checking capitals and spelling. Reading your essay aloud can help you find missing words and punctuation.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear shape: an introduction that lists three reasons, a paragraph for each reason, and a conclusion. Starting body paragraphs with 'My other reason' and 'Last but not the least' helps the reader follow along. Inside the paragraphs, though, ideas sometimes jump or repeat without a clear link. For example, the turtle and bunny comparison is not connected to your point about business people. Try adding a sentence that explains how each example supports your reason, and use transitions such as 'for example' or 'as a result'.

You use a mix of simple and compound sentences, and some sentences begin with 'Like what...' or 'When...'. Many sentences are short and follow the same pattern (Problems make us...). Some sentences are also unclear or hard to follow. Try combining ideas with words like 'because', 'although' or 'which', and vary how your sentences begin. Reread longer sentences to check that each one has a clear subject and verb.

Your word choices are mostly simple and easy to understand, and you use some good topic words such as 'goals' and 'mistakes'. A few words repeat many times ('problems', 'push harder', 'make us'). Some words are imprecise, such as 'big problem' and 'created'. Try using more exact words, such as 'challenge', 'obstacle', 'motivate', 'persevere' or 'overcome', to make your ideas stronger.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'learn from your mistakes', 'of course' and 'Last but not the least'. Other phrases do not sound natural in English, often because of the wrong preposition or word order. For example, English usually says 'agree with' rather than 'agree on', and 'these days' rather than 'this days'. The phrase 'work hard and hard' should be 'work harder and harder'. Collect common phrases when you read, and check which prepositions go with which verbs.

Your meaning is usually clear, but there are repeated grammar errors, especially subject-verb agreement and singular/plural forms. Examples are 'problems is', 'problem make', 'it make you' and 'a person have'. There are also some tense errors, such as 'I never seen my brother', which should be 'I had never seen' or 'I have not seen'. Check each sentence to see whether the subject is singular or plural and make the verb match. Also avoid switching between 'us' and 'you' in the same sentence.

Some of your punctuation is correct, and you use quotation marks to show other people's words. However, there are several spelling, capitalisation and punctuation problems. 'buisnessman' should be 'businessman'. 'Its' should be 'It's', 'their' should be 'they're' or 'there' depending on the meaning, and 'dont' needs an apostrophe. A space is missing after a comma in 'brother again,and'. You also capitalised every word in a quotation ('A Good Buisness-man Need Problems To Do Better'), and the slashes in 'work/push' are not standard in formal writing. Proofread slowly at the end, and choose one word instead of using a slash.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear structure: an introduction, one paragraph on respect, one on business, and a conclusion. Starting body paragraphs with 'One thing...' and 'Another thing...' helps the reader follow along. Some sentences inside the paragraphs do not connect smoothly. In the respect paragraph, the move from your father's past to your own childhood is abrupt, and the sentence trails off. Try transitions that explain the link, such as 'Because of this, he made sure that when I was old enough...'. The last sentence of the business paragraph restates the point in a confusing way. Make sure each paragraph ends by clearly tying back to your main idea.

You use a mix of simple sentences and some longer ones with 'because', 'but' and 'as well as'. That is a good start. Several longer sentences become tangled and lose control, so the reader has to guess your meaning. Try breaking these into two or three shorter sentences first, then combine them carefully. Also look at the incomplete sentence 'As well as listening to the adults, bow when entering a door and greeting them.' It needs a subject and a parallel structure.

Your word choice is mostly simple but clear, and you do include some useful words such as 'respectful', 'realized', 'experience' and 'wisdom'. You repeat 'showed', 'shared' and 'a person' very often. Try varied words like 'taught', 'demonstrated', 'explained' or 'guided'. Some words are also imprecise, such as 'trouble child' and 'bad choices'. More specific words (for example 'rebellious' or 'poor decisions') would make your ideas stronger.

You try several common phrases, such as 'For example', 'This shows that' and 'In conclusion', which helps your essay sound organized. Some word combinations are not natural in English. We say 'make bad choices', not 'do bad choices'. We say 'a lot of experience' rather than 'tones of experience'. 'Get respected into the family' is unclear, and 'bow when entering a door' is an unusual way to express your idea. Reading your sentences aloud and noting common word pairs ('make a choice', 'show respect', 'earn respect') will help.

Your meaning usually comes through, but there are frequent grammar errors that make parts hard to follow. Check these areas: verb forms after 'made' and 'make' ('made me realize'), subject-verb agreement ('I doesn't', 'people that is'), possessives and pronouns ('this parents' should be 'his parents'), and verb tense consistency ('was getting', 'had shared'). Also look for missing or extra words ('me to me like him' should be 'me to be like him'; 'show me' should be 'showed me'). Proofread slowly, one sentence at a time, looking only at the verbs.

Your essay has paragraphs and you use question marks and periods in many places. Several conventions need attention. Commas are often placed before a space instead of after the word ('mom ,grandparents', 'father ,because'). The pronoun 'I' is sometimes lowercase ('i was able'). Some sentences begin with a capital after a comma ('Soon when...'). There are spelling errors ('tones' for 'tons', 'though' for 'thought', 'experince', 'mange', 'like' for 'life') and a stray character ('H+e'). Proofreading for these small items will quickly make your writing look more polished.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear shape: an introduction, body paragraphs about sports, an instrument and chemistry, and a closing recommendation. Each body paragraph starts by naming a new activity, which helps the reader follow you. The links between ideas are often weak, though. You rely on 'because' and 'and' repeatedly, and the last paragraph does not clearly sum up your points. Try transitions such as 'for example', 'in addition' and 'in conclusion'. Also, make sure each paragraph stays on one idea. The chemistry paragraph moves from being excited to being afraid without a link between them.

You try different sentence types, including sentences with 'because', 'but' and 'before', which is good. Several sentences run together without the punctuation or connecting words they need, so it is hard to see where one idea ends and the next begins. Practise splitting long sentences into two or three shorter ones, and use a clear subject and verb in each. For example, 'An activity can be fun is like playing a sport' needs rewriting so it has one main verb.

You use some good topic words, such as 'professional', 'orchestra', 'audience', 'soothing' and 'chemicals'. However, 'fun', 'cool', 'enjoyable' and 'alot of' appear again and again. Try more precise words, such as 'thrilling', 'rewarding' or 'challenging', and explain what makes the activity good. Also check word choice. 'Chores' was probably meant to be 'chorus', and 'verse' should be 'versus' or 'compete against'.

Some of your phrases sound natural, such as 'I cant wait to do it', 'a lot of options to choose from' and 'play music in front of the audience'. Others are not quite the usual English collocations. Check these: 'in this new year that we are now there', 'go to trips' (usually 'go on trips'), 'recommend you to go' (usually 'recommend that you go'), and 'be in a stage' (usually 'be on a stage'). Reading your sentences aloud can help you notice what sounds odd.

Your meaning is usually clear, and you use past tense well in your soccer story ('I played', 'I used to be bad'). Some errors remain. Check subject-verb agreement and word forms: 'their are' should be 'there are', and 'activitys' should be 'activities'. Watch tense too: 'i used to play an insturment the last three years' should be 'I have played an instrument for the last three years'. Also check missing words: 'that fits yoou right and that enjoyable' needs 'is' and a clearer structure.

The main areas to work on are spelling, capital letters and punctuation. Many words are misspelled, such as 'thosands', 'elemantary', 'aggresive', 'insturment', 'extreame', 'audiance' and 'chemisry'. The pronoun 'I' and the beginnings of sentences are often not capitalised. Some sentences are missing a full stop or a comma, and apostrophes are missing in words like 'im' and 'cant'. Proofread slowly at the end and use a spell checker or dictionary for words you're unsure of. Check that every sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

studentFacing: Your essay stays on the topic of advice, but the ideas are not organised into clear paragraphs. They run together in one block. Several sentences are joined with 'because' or 'sometimes' without a clear link, so the reader loses your main point. Try one paragraph per idea (for example: different viewpoints, learning from experience, making hard decisions). Start each with a topic sentence and use transitions such as 'for example' or 'in addition'. Also avoid repeating the same idea ('know in what they need to improve on next time' appears twice). Instead, build toward a conclusion.

You try longer sentences, which is good, but many are run-ons that string clauses together without clear boundaries. Some sentences are also incomplete or unclear in structure. Practise splitting long sentences into two or three shorter ones, then combine them with a conjunction or a relative clause. Your questions could also be built more carefully, with a clear question form and an answer that follows.

Your word choice is simple and understandable, but it repeats a lot. 'Advice', 'people', 'sometimes' and 'help' appear many times. You also use some good words, such as 'inspirational', 'motivated' and 'challenging'. Try more precise words, such as 'guidance', 'perspective', 'support' or 'reassurance'. Use synonyms to avoid repeating the same word within a sentence.

There are several unnatural word combinations, especially the extra word 'in' before 'advice' and 'experienced'. English says 'ask for advice', 'have experience of something' and 'go through something difficult'. Learn these phrases as units. Also check phrases like 'help them answer' and 'in what they need to improve'. Natural versions would be 'what they need to improve'.

Several grammar patterns need attention. Check the difference between the noun 'advice' and the verb 'advise'. Check subject-verb agreement ('advice can helps'), word forms ('be success' should be 'be successful', 'feel worry' should be 'feel worried', 'effect' should be 'affect'), and plurals ('multiple opinion' should be 'multiple opinions'). Also check 'there' and 'their', and 'the' and 'they'. Reading your work aloud and slowly can help you catch these.

Your spelling is mostly readable, but there are punctuation and capitalisation problems. Apostrophes are missing ('its' should be 'it's', 'persons' should be 'person's'). Sentences often lack full stops, and capital letters appear in the middle of a sentence ('Seeking'). Questions inside sentences need clearer punctuation and capitals. Also use commas to separate clauses and lists. Make sure each sentence starts with a capital and ends with a full stop.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear three-part shape (opening, development, conclusion), and you use linking phrases such as 'In addition to this prompt' and 'In conclusion'. However, the ideas inside paragraphs are often repeated rather than developed. The second paragraph restates the first (that first impressions are part of who we are) without adding new evidence. 'In conclusion to this paragraph' is also confusing, because a conclusion should sum up the whole essay. In the last paragraph your position shifts: you say first impressions are important, and then that we should not judge by them. Try to link these two ideas explicitly, for example with 'however' or 'for this reason'. Also check that 'it' and 'this' clearly refer to something specific.

You try longer, complex sentences with several clauses, which shows ambition. Many of them run on through comma chains and become hard to follow, so the main idea gets lost. The first sentence is an example, with its many added clauses. Vary your sentence length: after a long sentence, add a short, clear one. Splitting long sentences into two or three will also help you control the structure of each one.

Your vocabulary is understandable and fits the topic, with words such as 'judge', 'analyze', 'personalities' and 'prove'. You rely on general words and repeat 'first impression', 'change' and 'part of' many times, so the range is limited. Try more precise alternatives, such as 'perception', 'adapt', 'trait', 'assumption' or 'character'. Check spelling and word choice too: 'unic' should be 'unique' and 'change' in the last line should probably be 'chance'.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'a lot to me', 'thanks to my past experiences' and 'prove you're wrong'. Other phrases sound unnatural or come from a direct translation: 'better said similar', 'on my every day life', 'how my culture distinguish me' and 'their way to treat people'. Consider more natural options, such as 'in my daily life', 'how my culture shapes me' and 'the way they treat people'. Reading model essays and noting common word combinations will help.

Your meaning usually comes through, but some grammar errors recur. The main ones are missing subjects, as in 'because is part of ourselves', and subject-verb agreement, as in 'how my culture distinguish me'. There are also article errors ('an stranger'), and tense or modal use is sometimes unclear ('it won't change that easy', which needs 'easily'; 'it'll be because is part of'). Proofread for these patterns: always include a subject ('it is'), check the verb ending, and choose 'a' or 'an' by the next sound. The pronoun shift between 'we', 'I' and 'you' can also be confusing.

Your spelling is mostly correct, and your paragraphs are clearly separated. However, you write 'i' in lowercase several times when it should be capital 'I'. Comma splices (joining full sentences with only a comma) are frequent, and the long sentences contain few full stops. A colon is also used oddly in 'what I really mean by that is: First impression'. Read your essay aloud and put a full stop wherever you naturally pause to finish a thought. Also fix 'unic' and 'change/chance'.

studentFacing: Your essay is clearly organised. You use an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion, and you signal each step with transitions such as 'Firts', 'Next', 'Finally' and 'In sum'. Each paragraph begins with a topic sentence that links back to your thesis. To improve, vary your transitions and connect your ideas more closely within paragraphs. The repeated phrase 'always doing something' and the repeated 'Also' make the writing feel mechanical. Try showing how your points relate to each other, for example how staying busy prevents boredom and so supports health and goals.

You use some complex sentences, with 'because', 'if' and 'when' clauses, and these work well. However, many sentences follow the same pattern: 'we can... because we...'. Some are also very long and strung together with 'and'. Try varying your openings and using relative clauses or participial phrases. The second sentence of the introduction is also a problem. It is a statement that ends as a question structure, so it needs to be rewritten as a clear sentence.

Your vocabulary is clear and appropriate for the topic, but it is quite basic and repetitive. 'Do always something', 'good' and 'get bored' appear many times. Try more precise words, such as 'productive', 'motivated', 'stay engaged', 'maintain physical fitness', 'pursue goals' or 'sedentary'. Also check 'propose', which here should be 'set out to do' or 'aim for'.

Some of your phrases are natural, for example 'spend our time', 'pay attention' and 'fight for what we want'. Several other expressions are not idiomatic in English. The adverb 'always' is misplaced, and some collocations are unusual. Practise placing the adverb before the main verb ('we should always be doing something') and learning common collocations such as 'stay busy' and 'the day goes by faster'.

Your meaning is usually clear, but several grammar errors recur. Watch for: subject-verb agreement ('the day feel'), plural forms ('bodys', 'homeworks'), the gerund after a preposition ('focus on do' should be 'focus on doing'), word order ('do always something'), and a wrong pronoun ('to they gym' should be 'the gym'). Also, 'gona fight' should be 'are going to fight', and 'better persons' is more naturally 'better people'. Proofreading for these patterns would improve your accuracy considerably.

Your punctuation and paragraphing are generally sound, but there are repeated spelling errors and some capitalisation and punctuation slips. Check these words: 'Firts' (First), 'Addionally' (Additionally), 'excersises' (exercises), 'shool' (school), 'wat' (want), 'gona' (gonna/going to), 'its' (it's). Also, 'To conclude, It' should have a lowercase 'it', and 'We can can' has a repeated word. Add a comma after introductory phrases and before 'or' lists consistently. Reading your essay aloud slowly can help you catch these.

Try starting each paragraph with a clear main idea, using transitions such as 'for example' or 'as a result', and finishing with a sentence that ties back to your position.

Several sentences start with 'But', and some join two complete ideas without proper punctuation. Signposting phrases like 'My first reason why is' and 'My second reason is' make it easy to follow. The links between ideas are basic, though. Several sentences are joined by 'and' or a comma rather than by a transition that shows how the ideas relate. Try linking your points more precisely, for example by explaining how learning from an example leads to influence. Developing each paragraph with a specific example would also help the essay flow.

You use some complex sentences, such as ones with 'because', 'when' and 'depending on'. Several sentences are very long and run on, which makes the meaning hard to follow. Try splitting long sentences into two or three shorter ones. Vary how your sentences begin, and use a mix of simple and complex structures to keep control of your meaning.

Your word choice is mostly clear and appropriate, and 'comprehend', 'influence' and 'strive' are good choices. Some words are repetitive or vague, such as 'example', 'behavior', 'reasons' and 'smart'. Some phrases are imprecise, like 'self behavior examples'. Try more specific words, for example 'role model', 'inspire' or 'demonstrate', and replace 'smart adult' with something like 'a trusted mentor'.

Some phrases work well and sound natural, such as 'Nobody is perfect' and 'you'll be surprised by how many people'. Others are not quite idiomatic or are missing words. For example, 'the majority people around world' should be 'the majority of people around the world', and 'in front them' should be 'in front of them'. 'Act upon that action' repeats itself, and 'act upon there actions' would be better as 'follow their example'. Reading your work aloud can help you catch these.

The opening sentence is also unclear about what is 'better' than what. Proofread for small function words and for homophones.

Your paragraphs are clearly separated and most sentences start with capital letters. Remaining issues are spelling, apostrophes and punctuation. Check 'becuase' (because), 'youv'e' (you've), 'its okay' (it's okay) and 'everyday' (every day). Commas are missing after introductory phrases like 'In addition' and 'In conclusion'. In one place a comma is used where a full stop or a conjunction is needed ('like you,soon'), and a space is missing after it. Proofreading slowly at the end would fix many of these.

studentFacing: Your essay stays on one position (four years is better), and you use connectors like 'So' and 'But' to link paragraphs. However, the same reasons (family time, summer, work) repeat in almost every paragraph without building on each other. The first paragraph also mixes the idea of going to college with going to work in a way that is hard to follow. Try giving each paragraph one distinct reason, with a clear topic sentence, and use a wider range of transitions such as 'In addition', 'For example' or 'As a result'. The last paragraph is a single sentence, so it feels like an afterthought rather than a conclusion.

You attempt long, multi-clause sentences, which shows willingness to build complex ideas. Many of them run on through repeated 'and' and 'because' without clear control, which makes them hard to follow. Try splitting long sentences into two or three shorter ones, and vary your sentence openings and structures (for example, using a 'Although...' or 'If...' clause at the start).

Your word choice is simple and understandable, but it is quite repetitive. 'Time', 'chose', 'family' and 'graduate' appear many times. Try more precise words, such as 'flexibility', 'workload', 'burnout', 'opportunities' or 'balance', to express your ideas more exactly and avoid repeating yourself.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'back and forth' and 'all the time in the world', which add a conversational touch. Some phrases are used in ways that are not quite standard or that are too informal for an argumentative essay, such as 'so on and so forth' and 'straight into the work force'. Check the standard form of common collocations, such as 'workforce', 'take time off' and 'it is up to them'.

There are recurring errors with plurals, verb forms and missing words. Examples: 'student' instead of 'students', 'so many thing', 'four year', 'chose' where the base form 'choose' is needed, and a missing verb in 'It up to them'. There is also a missing 'to' in 'able spend'. Proofreading specifically for plural endings and for verb forms after 'to' would remove many of these errors.

Most words are spelled correctly, but there are several convention errors. There is a doubled word ('to to'), a missing 'f' ('time of' instead of 'time off'), a lowercase 'but' at the start of a paragraph, and a misplaced comma in 'sky,diving'. Commas are also missing in lists ('your family your relative and your friends'). Reading your essay aloud can help you notice where punctuation is needed.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear shape: an introduction, body paragraphs that use transitions such as 'Furthermore', 'Moreover' and 'Overall', and a conclusion that restates your main points. The ideas within paragraphs sometimes drift, though. In the second paragraph, the story about your girlfriend moves between several points (being new, panic attacks, doing homework) without a clear link back to your claim about online school. The last body paragraph on drama also feels loosely connected to your earlier points about safety and sickness. Try ending each paragraph with a sentence that ties the example back to your main argument. Also, 'Moreover' is used twice, so vary your transitions.

You use a good variety of sentence types, including complex sentences with subordinate clauses and some longer sentences that combine several ideas. Some of these long sentences become hard to follow or are joined with only a comma (a comma splice). Others have a structure that doesn't quite work. Check long sentences to be sure each clause fits together, and split them where needed.

Your word choice is mostly clear and suits the topic, and a few words stand out, such as 'distractions', 'beneficial' and 'scholars'. However, you rely on simple, repeated words and phrases ('important information or work', 'safe', 'very'). Some word choices are imprecise, for example 'the advances of the students' and 'the advances of our present civilization'. Try replacing general words with more specific ones, and check that each word means what you intend.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'miss out on', 'no matter where it is' and 'take this distraction out of their equation', which give your writing a personal voice. There are also several collocation problems and awkward phrasings. The phrase 'very often panic attacks' puts the adverb in an unusual place, and the phrase 'talking up and down and all around the school' is unclear. Try 'frequent panic attacks' or 'she often has panic attacks'. Reading your essay aloud can help you hear which phrases sound unnatural.

Your meaning is usually clear, but several grammar errors recur. These include subject-verb agreement ('drama is one major factor on why students wishes'), word form and word choice ('then their peers' instead of 'than'), missing articles or prepositions, and tense and form errors ('for they day'). There is also a tense inconsistency in the story about your girlfriend, where you move between past and present. Proofread for agreement and word forms, and keep verb tense consistent within an example.

Your paragraphs are clearly marked and most sentences begin with capital letters and end with correct punctuation. Several convention errors remain: 'going through out' should be 'throughout', 'When ever' should be 'Whenever', 'i'm' should be 'I'm', and 'Imagine' is capitalized mid-sentence. 'face time' should be 'FaceTime'. Commas are sometimes missing or misplaced, and a semicolon is used after 'For example' where a comma would be correct. A careful proofread focusing on these patterns would improve this area quickly.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear overall structure: an introduction, two body paragraphs introduced with 'Firstly' and 'Secondly', and a conclusion that restates your two reasons (feelings and concrete action). Within paragraphs, the links between ideas are weaker. Some transitions are used loosely, and some sentences repeat the same idea instead of moving it forward. Pronoun reference also slips between 'you', 'him', 'them' and 'your speaker'. Try choosing one perspective and keeping to it. Link your examples back to your claim, for instance by explaining how Martin Luther King's words show the power of feelings.

You attempt a variety of structures, including subordinate clauses ('Although people disagree with... people should consider that...'), purpose clauses and relative clauses. This shows ambition. Control is uneven, though. Some sentences are overlong and stack several clauses with 'because' or 'and', and some are awkward or incomplete in structure. Try splitting long sentences and checking that each one has a clear subject and verb.

You use some good topic words such as 'persuade', 'influence', 'solemn' and 'humanitarian'. However, several words are imprecise or not quite right, and the same words ('feelings', 'example', 'behavior', 'convince') repeat often. 'Sensitivity', 'the concrete', 'publicity' and 'speaker' are used in unusual ways, probably transferred from your first language. Consider more precise choices such as 'emotion', 'tangible evidence', 'advertising' and 'audience'.

Several expressions are direct translations and do not sound natural in English. Others have collocation problems. Good alternatives would be 'set a good example', 'lead by example', 'appeal to emotions' and 'the best way to persuade'. Pay attention to which prepositions and articles normally go with a word. You do use some fixed phrases correctly, such as 'For instance', 'In this way' and 'in order to'.

Meaning is usually understandable, but there are frequent errors in word forms, articles, agreement and comparatives. Check the following: 'success' used as a verb (should be 'succeed'), 'can be persuade' (should be 'persuaded'), 'the better way' (should be 'the best way' or 'a better way'), 'an humanitarian' (should be 'a humanitarian'), and 'there is not better way'. Articles are often added where English omits them ('the fear, the happiness', 'the fashion', 'the politics'). Several verb patterns also need fixing, such as 'help him to trust you' and 'prefer doing it in the shop instead of in line'. Proofreading for one error type at a time can help.

Your paragraphing, capitalisation and sentence-ending punctuation are mostly sound. Some errors remain: 'trough' for 'through', 'the World War II' (should be 'World War II'), and 'musics' (the noun is uncountable). A comma is misplaced in 'a serious, and sad speech'. Also check how you introduce and punctuate quotations. A final proofread with a spelling check would catch many of these.

studentFacing: Your essay has four paragraphs, and you return to the idea of family and friends, which gives it a loose focus. However, the ideas do not connect clearly. You move from sharks to skydiving to memories without transitions that explain how they relate. Words like 'because' are repeated and 'also', 'for example', or 'however' would help. The last paragraph does not conclude your main point. Try to begin each paragraph with a sentence that states its main idea, then support it with a reason or example.

You mostly use simple sentences and 'because' clauses, and you try a contrast with 'but', which is a good start. Several sentences are incomplete or unclear in structure, such as the one that begins with 'Doing your favorite activite'. Try varying your sentences, for example by starting with a phrase ('When I am with my family, ...') and checking that every sentence has a subject and a verb.

Your word choice is basic and often repeated, especially 'fun', 'love', 'things', 'stuff' and 'activities'. The ideas would be stronger with more precise words, such as 'thrilling', 'memorable', 'overcome', or 'challenge'. Notice also that 'bad' in 'Doing things that get you over fear is bad' probably does not mean what you intended. Check that your word matches your meaning.

You use some natural phrases, such as 'get over your fear' and 'with or without family and friends', which is good. Other phrases are not quite standard English. For example, 'swim with sharks' needs 'to' ('to swim with sharks'), and 'have other opinion' should be 'have different opinions'. Learn common collocations like 'accomplish a goal', 'overcome a fear', and 'make memories'.

There are frequent errors that sometimes make your meaning hard to follow. You miss words ('would like accomplish' should be 'would like to accomplish'), use singular where plural is needed ('family and friend', 'other opinion'), and have agreement errors ('The activites you do is all fun' should be 'are'). Also check 'is swim' (should be 'to swim') and 'the like or not like' (should be 'they like or do not like'). Reading your work aloud can help you find these.

There are many spelling, capitalisation and punctuation errors. Words to check: 'alot' (a lot), 'swiming' (swimming), 'allthogether' (all together), 'activite/activetes' (activities), 'allways' (always), and 'foing' (doing). Sentences should start with capital letters ('skydiving', 'lot of stuff', 'all the activetes'). Add apostrophes ('won't') and a question mark to your first sentence, since it is a question. Proofreading slowly at the end would fix many of these.

You use ordinal transitions (First, Second, Third, In conclusion) and 'For example' to guide the reader. The pattern is very repetitive, though, and 'First' is used twice in the same paragraph, which blurs the sequence. Some links between ideas are also weak. In the language paragraph, 'they could be the only one that learned that language' is not clearly tied to your claim. Try varying your transitions (for instance 'Moreover', 'In addition', 'As a result') and explaining how each example supports your main argument. The reference to 'your class' also shifts the point of view away from 'students'.

You mostly use simple and compound sentences, and a few complex ones with 'because' and 'unlike'. Several sentences are well controlled. Many sentences begin the same way ('First,... For example,...'), so the rhythm feels repetitive. Some sentences are also incomplete or awkwardly built, such as 'For example, a student is sick or had a docters appointment they could make up that work'. Try combining short ideas into more varied complex sentences, and check that each sentence has a clear subject and verb.

Your word choice is clear and appropriate for the topic, and words like 'advantage', 'communicate' and 'struggling' work well. Much of the vocabulary is general, though, and some words are repeated often ('time', 'students', 'activity', 'could'). More precise words would strengthen your argument, for example 'academic performance' instead of 'better in school', or 'obligation' instead of 'have to have an activity'. The informal ending 'Go stop extracurriculars!' also doesn't fit an argumentative essay.

You use some natural expressions, such as 'spend time with family and friends', 'make up that work' and 'quality time'. Others are not quite idiomatic or sound conversational: 'There is other to life then school and activities', 'grow you a stronger relashionship' and 'take half of the students time with going to school'. Reading model essays and noting common collocations (for example 'build stronger relationships', 'there is more to life than...') would help.

Your meaning is usually understandable, but there are recurring grammar errors. Watch subject-verb agreement ('a student that have two or three languages', 'any student that do not want'), word forms and word choice ('then' for 'than', 'word' for 'world', 'around other that speak'), and verb forms (the missing 'to' in 'to not have' is fine, but 'make them' is a stray verb). Also keep your pronouns consistent: you switch between 'students/they' and 'you/your'. Proofread by reading aloud and checking each verb against its subject.

There are frequent spelling errors, some repeated: 'diffrenet', 'applecation', 'colloge' (twice), 'docters', 'eachother', 'relashionship', 'advantges', and 'word' for 'world'. Punctuation also needs attention. There is a missing space after commas ('dinner,or help'), extra spaces before commas ('a movie ,or'), and a misplaced space before a period ('homework .I'). Apostrophes are missing in 'students time', 'students weak part' and 'docters'. Capitalise the game names consistently and use a spell-checker, then proofread for spacing and apostrophes.
